function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below you’ll find everything you need to get **nodejs‑welcome** running inside a Docker container, exposed through a minimal Kubernetes deployment/service, and automatically built whenever something lands on the *main* branch via GitHub Actions.  
I’ve broken it down into the four “steps” you listed so you can follow along easily from your own terminal.

> ⚠️ **Important:** These instructions assume you already have SSH keys set up for `git@github.com` and that you’re able to push back to the repository. If not, please configure them first (`ssh-keygen`, add public key to GitHub, test connectivity).

---

## Step 1 – Clone the Repository  

```bash
# From an empty folder or wherever you keep your projects
$ git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
$ cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH:

```bash
$ git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
```

Check out the latest state of `main` just to be safe:

```bash
$ git checkout main
$ git pull origin main
```

---

## Step 2 – Analyse & Generate Artifacts  

### 2.1 Inspect What’s Inside

Run a quick scan to see what the project contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Node.js dependencies + start script |
| `app.js` *(or similar)* | Entry point of the server |
| `.env.example` | Example environment variables |

Open `package.json` to confirm the entry point:

```json
{
  ...
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js",
    ...
  }
}
```

Assuming the main file is `index.js`. Adjust paths below if yours differ.

---

### 2.2 Dockerfile

Create (or overwrite) `Dockerfile` at the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

COPY . .

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:20-alpine

ENV NODE_ENV production
EXPOSE 3000          # <-- adjust if your app uses another port

WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app .
CMD ["npm","run","start"]
```

#### Why this one?

| Layer | Reason |
|-------|--------|
| `node:20-alpine` | Small footprint, modern LTS |
| Separate build/runtime stages | Keeps runtime image lean (no dev deps) |
| `npm ci` | Guarantees reproducible installs |
| Exposing `3000` | Most tutorials use 3000; change if needed |

Save the file as `Dockerfile`.

---

### 2.3 Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Create a new directory called `k8s` (you may choose another location):

```bash
mkdir -p k8s && touch k8s/deploy.yaml
```

Add the following YAML to `k8s/deploy.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2                     # scale horizontally
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest     # replace with real registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000                            # same as EXPOSE above
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-welcome-secrets                # optional secrets
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # Change to ClusterIP/NodePort if preferred
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                   # Ingress/external-facing port
    targetPort: 3000           # Container's listening port
```

> **Tip:** Replace `ghcr.io/...` with whatever registry you plan to publish to (e.g., Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR). You can also embed the image directly in the CI pipeline without publishing externally—just reference the local image during tests.

---

### 2.4 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a new file under `.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yml
name: Build & Push Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      packages: write       # Needed for GHCR
      id-token: write       # For OIDC auth (optional)

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Packages
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache NPM modules
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-npm-

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:build-cache
          cache-to: type=inline
          load: false
          push: true

      - name: Update K8s manifests (Optional)
        run: echo "Your manifest update logic goes here"

```

#### Explanation

| Section | Why it matters |
|---------|----------------|
| `permissions:` | Grants token rights to push images to GHCR. |
| `actions/docker-login-action` | Authenticates against GHCR using the automatic `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. |
| `docker/build-push-action` | Builds multi‑stage Dockerfile, caches layers, tags with SHA, and pushes. |
| Optional “update K8s manifests” step | If you’d like to bump image tags in your `deploy.yaml` automatically, insert a small shell script or use a tool such as `sed` or `kubectl patch`. |

Feel free to tweak the image tag strategy (semver vs SHA) depending on your release process.

---

## Step 3 – Stage All Changes

Back in the repo root:

```bash
$ git status
# Should show Dockerfile, k8s/deploy.yaml, .github/workflows/build.yml added

$ git add Dockerfile k8s/deploy.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

(Optionally review diffs before committing.)

---

## Step 4 – Commit & Push

```bash
$ git commit -m "CI/CD: Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
$ git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, building the image and pushing it to GHCR. Your Kubernetes cluster can now consume the updated image via the `deploy.yaml` you created.

--- 

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✔︎ | Repo cloned locally |
| ✔︎ | Dockerfile written |
| ✔︎ | `k8s/deploy.yaml` ready |
| ✔︎ | GitHub Actions workflow configured |
| ✔︎ | Files staged, committed, and pushed |

That’s it! 🎉 Now you have a fully automated build pipeline and deployable artifacts for the **nodejs‑welcome** project. Happy coding!
